messages.subject: User specified model; independent pathways model for subsequent Q calculations
parts:
To all,

My models are as follows tested with first 10 snps:

# User specified model (factor loading for PHENO1 > 1)
modelCF<-"F1 =~ PHENO1 + PHENO2 + PHENO3
PHENO1 ~~ a*PHENO1
a > .001
F1 ~ SNP"
pfactorCF <- userGWAS(covstruc = LDSCoutput, SNPs = p_sumstats_test, model = modelCF, sub=c("F1~SNP"))

# Alt user specified model (factor loading for PHENO1 > 1)
modelCFalt <-"F1 =~ NA*PHENO1 + PHENO2 + PHENO3
F1 ~~1*F1
PHENO1 ~~ a*PHENO1
a > .001
F1 ~ SNP"
pfactorCFalt <- userGWAS(covstruc = LDSCoutput, SNPs = p_sumstats_test, model = modelCFalt, sub=c("F1~SNP"))

# Independent pathways model - to calculate Q
modelIPM<-"F1 =~ NA*PHENO1 + PHENO2 + PHENO3
F1 ~~1*F1
PHENO1 ~~ a*PHENO1
a > .001
PHENO1 + PHENO2 + PHENO3 ~ SNP"
pfactorIPM <- userGWAS(covstruc = LDSCoutput, SNPs = p_sumstats_test, model = modelIPM)

I have 2 questions:  
1. What is the difference between modelCF and modelCFalt?  I added the F1~~1*F1 and NA* for first phenotype, thinking that it was redundant to modelCF specification  (PHENO1 ~~ a*PHENO1 and a > .001).  The estimates and SEs are different by approximately a factor of 4.11 (but approximately) with approximately the same Z and Pval_Estimates.

2. For the Independent pathways model, as set up, generates 10 lines for each SNP (for each permutation e.g. F1=~PHENO1, F1=~PHENO2, F1=~PHENO3, PHENO1~~PHENO1, PHENO1~SNP, ..., F1~~F1), with different values for est, se, etc, but same chisq and chisq_df=0.  I figure there is something wrong with my model specification or the userGWAS code. 

Thanks!

Dan

messages.author: d6d83e22ef3ba9f1
messages.subject: Re: User specified model; independent pathways model for subsequent Q calculations
parts:
Hi Dan, 

Good questions! 

1. The difference is how the estimates are scaled. So in modelCF unit loading identification is automatically being used where the loading of the first indicator on the factor is fixed to 1, and then all the estimates are going to shift around to reflect that loading. In modelCFalt you are specifying unit variance identification where the variance of the factor is fixed to 1 and that first loading is freely estimated. They are statistically equivalent, just different ways of scaling the estimates, which is why you get the same p-values and z-statistics. 

2. If you don't specify anything for the sub argument, then userGWAS will save all components of the model for each SNP (not recommended just for memory reasons). So for each SNP it is showing the full set of model results, and then printing the same model chi-square on each line since this is the model fit for the same model (a bit confusing I know, but we figured it was better than having a completely separate list object of model fit indices that you then have to match up with each SNP). 

Best, 
  Andrew

messages.subject: Re: User specified model; independent pathways model for subsequent Q calculations
parts:
Responding to both Sarah and Dan here: 

Dan, my guess is you have at least one variable that has a residual variance in the model without individual SNPs that is close enough to 0 that in the model with the SNPs that in some rare cases you end up with the negative variance warnings you are highlighting. If it's a really small proportion of your SNPs, then you could consider just excluding them. My honest response is I could see going either way as far as whether you run them through userGWAS with the constraints or just drop them, but would probably go with the userGWAS option myself. 

Sarah, you are correct that just taking the chisq on the common pathways model for a 3 df factor is equal to the Q_SNP index. When you say all of the chi-square values are significant are you using 5e-8 as the significance threshold? 

-Andrew

It looks like the issue is that you are still getting a fair amount of misfit for the part of the model that should not be contributing to overall mode chi-square. More specifically, the constraint on the residual variance for Phenotype 2 is causing misfit for that part of the matrix, and you can see that the model chi-square drops to nonsignificant across the example SNPs you sent if you remove the constraints on the residual variance. This hasn't come up before because for models with multiple factors or with a single factor with > 3 indicators, Q_SNP is still calculated by comparing the model chi-square estimates across the common and independent pathways models and the chi-square contribution for misfit caused due to constraints on the residual variances simply cancels out across those comparisons. However, as you correctly pointed out in your earlier question, for a 3 indicator you should in theory just be able to run the common pathways model since the independent pathways model is fully saturated, but that has yielded the issue you ran into where that misfit doesn't cancel out and you get the highly significant model chi-square for all SNPs. So that's why the issue is arising and I can see a couple of options in this instance: 

1. You could remove the constraints on the residual variances and note that this is an interpretive limitation of the model that it produces the negative residual

You could fix the residual variance to 0 to mirror what the constraint is effectively doing and so that the independent pathways model is no longer fully saturated and you can then do the model chi-square comparison such that misfit due to Phenotype_2 cancels out across the models as would typically happen in these sorts of instances. a > 0.001
PHENO2 ~~ 0*PHENO2
PHENO3 ~~ c*PHENO3
c > 0.001
F1~SNP'

a > 0.001
PHENO2 ~~ 0*PHENO2
PHENO3 ~~ c*PHENO3
c > 0.001
PHENO1 + PHENO2 + PHENO3~SNP'

It makes sense, given the observed data, that you then end up with model estimates where it is trying to push the factor loading for Pheno2 up to a point where the residual variance goes negative since it correlates so much stronger with the other traits. Best, 
  Andrew

Hi Sarah, 

Just to be clear, option 2 requires doing the model comparison across the common and independent pathways model since the independent pathways model is no longer fully saturated. Two points to consider in response to your question: 

1. Whether filtering on Q is the appropriate approach for downstream analysis on the factor depends somewhat on the analysis you want to do. For example, if you are examining functional enrichment, I would recommend estimating that directly within the model using Stratified Genomic SEM. I know for others a research question of interest is how the factor correlates with other external traits. In that case, I would estimate the LDSC object using that external trait and estimate the genetic correlations within the model itself since those will be unbiased by heterogeneity in SNP-level signal. That said, if your planned follow-up analyses falls outside of these two instances then yes filtering on Q_SNP would be the way to go. 

2. If you are filtering out Q_SNPs for downstream analyses on the multivariate GWAS summary statistics for a factor you might consider also filtering out SNPs in LD with the signifiant Q_hits at some R^2 threshold (e.g., > 0.6). 

Best, 
  Andrew

Hi Sarah, 

Thanks for sending along the code and data files! I'm just replying here so others who run into this issue can see the response and also because there may be varying opinions out there on this one so if anyone else on the Genomic SEM team or otherwise wants to weigh in please feel free. 

It looks like the issue is that you are still getting a fair amount of misfit for the part of the model that should not be contributing to overall mode chi-square. More specifically, the constraint on the residual variance for Phenotype 2 is causing misfit for that part of the matrix, and you can see that the model chi-square drops to nonsignificant across the example SNPs you sent if you remove the constraints on the residual variance. This hasn't come up before because for models with multiple factors or with a single factor with > 3 indicators, Q_SNP is still calculated by comparing the model chi-square estimates across the common and independent pathways models and the chi-square contribution for misfit caused due to constraints on the residual variances simply cancels out across those comparisons. However, as you correctly pointed out in your earlier question, for a 3 indicator you should in theory just be able to run the common pathways model since the independent pathways model is fully saturated, but that has yielded the issue you ran into where that misfit doesn't cancel out and you get the highly significant model chi-square for all SNPs. So that's why the issue is arising and I can see a couple of options in this instance: 

1. You could remove the constraints on the residual variances and note that this is an interpretive limitation of the model that it produces the negative residual 

2. You could fix the residual variance to 0 to mirror what the constraint is effectively doing and so that the independent pathways model is no longer fully saturated and you can then do the model chi-square comparison such that misfit due to Phenotype_2 cancels out across the models as would typically happen in these sorts of instances. Example code for what I'm suggesting here is below: 

common_mod <- 'F1 =~ PHENO1 + PHENO2 + PHENO3
PHENO1 ~~ a*PHENO1
a > 0.001
PHENO2 ~~ 0*PHENO2
PHENO3 ~~ c*PHENO3
c > 0.001
F1~SNP'

common_factor <- userGWAS(covstruc = LDSCoutput_COG_v2, SNPs = sumstats_5SNPs,sub=c("F1~SNP"), model = common_mod, parallel = F)

ind_mod <- 'F1 =~ PHENO1 + PHENO2 + PHENO3
PHENO1 ~~ a*PHENO1
a > 0.001
PHENO2 ~~ 0*PHENO2
PHENO3 ~~ c*PHENO3
c > 0.001
PHENO1 + PHENO2 + PHENO3~SNP'

ind_factor <- userGWAS(covstruc = LDSCoutput_COG_v2, SNPs = sumstats_5SNPs, sub="PHENO1~SNP",model = ind_mod, parallel = F)

Q_SNP<-pchisq(common_factor[[1]]$chisq-ind_factor[[1]]$chisq,common_factor[[1]]$chisq_df-ind_factor[[1]]$chisq_df,lower.tail=FALSE)

3. You can revisit the choice of traits included in your model and try to find an additional trait or traits to include in your model. If you look at the genetic correlation matrix across your traits, Pheno 2 correlates at .7 across the other two traits, while Pheno1 and Pheno3 correlate at .3. It makes sense, given the observed data, that you then end up with model estimates where it is trying to push the factor loading for Pheno2 up to a point where the residual variance goes negative since it correlates so much stronger with the other traits. I know this is next to impossible to do as for as a prior trait selection, but if you had some sense of other traits that you could include that correlate more strongly with Pheno 1 or 3, or correlate moderate to strong with all three phenotypes, that would help balance out the "centrality" of Pheno2 in your factor. 

Best, 
  Andrew

On Wednesday, July 27, 2022 at 4:04:36 PM UTC-4 agro...@gmail.com wrote:
Hi Dan, 

Good questions! 

1. The difference is how the estimates are scaled. So in modelCF unit loading identification is automatically being used where the loading of the first indicator on the factor is fixed to 1, and then all the estimates are going to shift around to reflect that loading. In modelCFalt you are specifying unit variance identification where the variance of the factor is fixed to 1 and that first loading is freely estimated. They are statistically equivalent, just different ways of scaling the estimates, which is why you get the same p-values and z-statistics. 

2. If you don't specify anything for the sub argument, then userGWAS will save all components of the model for each SNP (not recommended just for memory reasons). So for each SNP it is showing the full set of model results, and then printing the same model chi-square on each line since this is the model fit for the same model (a bit confusing I know, but we figured it was better than having a completely separate list object of model fit indices that you then have to match up with each SNP). 

Best, 
  Andrew

It looks like the issue is that you are still getting a fair amount of misfit for the part of the model that should not be contributing to overall mode chi-square. More specifically, the constraint on the residual variance for Phenotype 2 is causing misfit for that part of the matrix, and you can see that the model chi-square drops to nonsignificant across the example SNPs you sent if you remove the constraints on the residual variance. This hasn't come up before because for models with multiple factors or with a single factor with > 3 indicators, Q_SNP is still calculated by comparing the model chi-square estimates across the common and independent pathways models and the chi-square contribution for misfit caused due to constraints on the residual variances simply cancels out across those comparisons. However, as you correctly pointed out in your earlier question, for a 3 indicator you should in theory just be able to run the common pathways model since the independent pathways model is fully saturated, but that has yielded the issue you ran into where that misfit doesn't cancel out and you get the highly significant model chi-square for all SNPs. 1. You could remove the constraints on the residual variances and note that this is an interpretive limitation of the model that it produces the negative residual 

2. You could fix the residual variance to 0 to mirror what the constraint is effectively doing and so that the independent pathways model is no longer fully saturated and you can then do the model chi-square comparison such that misfit due to Phenotype_2 cancels out across the models as would typically happen in these sorts of instances. a > 0.001

PHENO3 ~~ c*PHENO3

Hi Dan, 

Good questions! 

1. The difference is how the estimates are scaled. So in modelCF unit loading identification is automatically being used where the loading of the first indicator on the factor is fixed to 1, and then all the estimates are going to shift around to reflect that loading. In modelCFalt you are specifying unit variance identification where the variance of the factor is fixed to 1 and that first loading is freely estimated. They are statistically equivalent, just different ways of scaling the estimates, which is why you get the same p-values and z-statistics. 

2. If you don't specify anything for the sub argument, then userGWAS will save all components of the model for each SNP (not recommended just for memory reasons). So for each SNP it is showing the full set of model results, and then printing the same model chi-square on each line since this is the model fit for the same model (a bit confusing I know, but we figured it was better than having a completely separate list object of model fit indices that you then have to match up with each SNP).
